questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mean, median, and mode as measures of center?
options: The median is the most sensitive to extreme outliers because it uses the exact value of every observation.
The mean is the balance point of the data and uses every value, while the median only depends on the ordering of values and is therefore robust to outliers.
The mode can only be computed for numerical data, never for categorical data.
When the mean and median differ substantially, it indicates the dataset contains no outliers.
The median is computed by averaging all values and dividing by the count, while the mean is the middle value after sorting.
A trimmed mean discards all but the single middle value, making it identical to the median.
questions.explain: The mean sums every value and divides by the count, so one extreme value pulls it substantially; the median only depends on where values rank, so an outlier barely moves it. This is why a large gap between mean and median is treated as a warning sign for skew or outliers rather than something to ignore.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A reverses the actual sensitivity: it is the mean that reacts strongly to extreme values, because it incorporates the exact size of every observation in its calculation. The median only cares about rank order, so an extreme value just becomes 'one more value on the high end' — which is exactly why the median is called robust, not the mean.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: dividing a sample's squared deviations by n minus 1 instead of n is called the sample variance, and this adjustment is known as ________'s correction.
questions.explain: Dividing by n systematically underestimates the true population variance because a sample's values sit closer to their own mean than to the population mean; dividing by n minus 1 instead corrects for this bias, which is why the adjustment is named Bessel's correction, and why pandas' .var() defaults to ddof=1 while numpy's np.var() defaults to ddof=0.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about skewness and shape, per Lesson 5.
options: In a right-skewed distribution, the mean tends to sit above the median.
A distribution's skewness number near 0 always means the data has only one peak.
Kurtosis compares the weight of a distribution's tails to that of a normal distribution, with 0 as the excess-kurtosis baseline.
Applying a logarithm transform to a right-skewed positive variable can reduce its skewness.
A bimodal distribution's mean and median will always be noticeably different from each other.
questions.explain: Right-skewed data pulls the mean above the median because the mean reacts to the long tail while the median does not. Excess kurtosis, as pandas computes it, treats 0 as the normal-distribution baseline for tail weight. A log transform compresses a long right tail and can bring skewness much closer to 0, as Lesson 5 showed with the right-skewed example (skew falling from about 1.97 to about -0.47). A skewness near 0 does not guarantee unimodal data, and a bimodal distribution's mean and median are not guaranteed to differ either — the lesson's two-cluster courier example had a mean and median both near 40, almost identical to each other, even though a histogram clearly showed two separate peaks far from 40.

questions.prompt: A data scientist computes both the mean and median of a column of customer order values and finds the mean is nearly three times larger than the median. Based on Chapter 1, what should this gap make the analyst suspect, and what should they do next?
options: The data is likely right-skewed or contains outliers pulling the mean upward; the analyst should look at a histogram or box plot before reporting either number alone.
The data entry must contain an error, since a correctly collected column can never produce a mean and median that far apart.
The gap means the mean was calculated incorrectly, since the mean and median should always be nearly equal for any real dataset.
The gap is irrelevant to the shape of the data; it only affects which chart type is legal to draw.
questions.explain: A mean well above the median is the classic fingerprint of a right-skewed distribution or outliers, because the mean uses every value's exact size while the median only uses rank. Lesson 3's nine-order example showed exactly this: one 400-dollar order pulled the mean to 61.89 while the median stayed at 20. The right move is to look at the shape with a chart before trusting either single number, not to assume a data error or ignore the signal.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement scale to the example that illustrates it, per Lesson 2.
right: Order value in dollars, where zero means no order and $80 is twice $40
Payment method (credit card, PayPal, cash), with no inherent order
Temperature in Celsius, where equal gaps are meaningful but zero is arbitrary
Customer satisfaction rated low/medium/high, ordered but with unequal gaps
questions.explain: Nominal data is labels with no order, like payment method. Ordinal data has a meaningful order but unequal gaps, like a low/medium/high satisfaction rating. Interval data has equal gaps but no true zero, like Celsius temperature. Ratio data has both equal gaps and a true zero, like order value in dollars, where zero means none and ratios like 'twice as much' are meaningful.

questions.prompt: A rare disease affects 1 percent of a population. A test for it has a 90 percent sensitivity (correctly flags 90 percent of true cases) and a 5 percent false positive rate on healthy people. A patient tests positive. Based on Bayes' theorem, which statement correctly describes their situation?
options: Despite the positive result, the patient is still more likely to not have the disease than to have it, because the disease's low base rate means false positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives from the small diseased group.
The patient is approximately 90 percent likely to have the disease, since that is the test's sensitivity.
The patient is approximately 95 percent likely to have the disease, since that is 100 percent minus the false positive rate.
The base rate of the disease is irrelevant once a positive test result is observed.
questions.explain: Using natural frequencies on 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and the test catches 90 of them; of the 9,900 healthy people, 5 percent (about 495) still test positive. Out of 90 + 495 = 585 positive results, only 90 are true cases, so P(disease | positive) is about 90/585, roughly 15 percent, still more likely not to have the disease than to have it. This mirrors Lesson 9's fraud detector, where a 95 percent sensitive test with a 2 percent false positive rate on a 0.5 percent base rate produced only a 19.3 percent posterior; ignoring the small base rate is exactly the base rate fallacy.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about conditional probability and independence, per Lesson 8.
options: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are generally different questions with different answers.
If two events are mutually exclusive, they must also be independent, since neither depends on the other.
Events A and B are independent exactly when P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B).
Assuming observations are independent is always a safe default in real data, since most real-world events are unrelated.
Conditioning on an event is equivalent to filtering the data down to just the rows where that event is true, then computing a mean or proportion within that subset.
questions.explain: P(A | B) and P(B | A) answer different questions and are generally not equal — Lesson 8's plan/churn table showed P(churn | Free) = 0.3 while P(Free | churn) = 0.75. Independence is formally defined by P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Conditioning really is just filtering to the subset where B happened and then summarizing, exactly how groupby works in pandas. Mutually exclusive events are not independent — if one happens the other becomes impossible, which is itself a strong dependency, not an absence of one. And the lesson explicitly warns against assuming independence as a safe default, since customers in the same household or repeated measurements over time are frequently correlated.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), the subtraction is necessary because adding P(A) and P(B) directly counts the ________ twice.
questions.explain: If you add P(A) and P(B) directly, any outcome that belongs to both events gets counted once inside P(A) and again inside P(B), double-counting the overlap. Subtracting P(A and B) removes that double-count exactly once, leaving each outcome counted a single time. When A and B are mutually exclusive, the overlap is zero and the rule simplifies to simple addition.

questions.prompt: A raffle ticket costs $5 and has a 1-in-40 chance of winning a $150 prize. Using expected value as in Lesson 10, what is the expected net gain per ticket, and what does that number mean for someone who buys many tickets over time?
options: Expected net gain is (150 x 1/40) - 5 = -1.25 dollars per ticket; over many tickets, the player should expect to lose money on average, even though any single ticket might win.
Expected net gain is (150 x 1/40) - 5 = -1.25 dollars per ticket; this guarantees every individual player will lose exactly 1.25 dollars.
Expected net gain is 150 - 5 = 145 dollars per ticket, since the full prize should be counted regardless of the odds.
Expected net gain cannot be computed without knowing how many tickets will be sold in total.
questions.explain: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability: (150 x 1/40) - 5 = 3.75 - 5 = -1.25 dollars per ticket. That is a long-run average, not a guarantee for any one person — exactly the distinction Lesson 10 draws when it notes expected value is a long-run average, not a prediction for any single trial. Over many tickets, the player should expect to come out behind, which is also why a business running such a raffle profits on average.

questions.prompt: A website wants to model how many visitors convert out of the next 50 visitors, where each visitor converts independently with the same 8 percent probability. Which distribution correctly models the total count of conversions, and why?
options: Binomial, because it counts the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability.
Poisson, because conversions are being counted and Poisson always applies whenever you are counting something.
Geometric, because it models how many visitors you wait through before the first conversion.
Exponential, because it models the time between independent events arriving at a steady rate.
questions.explain: The binomial distribution counts successes across a fixed number n of independent trials that each share the same success probability p, exactly 50 visitors each with an 8 percent chance. Poisson instead counts events in a window with no fixed n, and is actually the limit of a binomial with huge n and tiny p, not a default for every counting problem. Geometric counts trials until the first success, and exponential models the continuous gap between events; neither matches a fixed count of 50 trials.

questions.prompt: Match each distribution to the situation it is built to model, per Chapter 3.
right: The number of help-desk tickets arriving in a fixed one-hour window, at a steady average rate
The waiting time between two consecutive events arriving at a steady average rate
A bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails than normal, used when the spread must be estimated from a small sample
A right-skewed distribution built from sums of squared normal values, used to compare a test statistic rather than to model raw data
questions.explain: Poisson counts events in a fixed window at a steady rate, like tickets per hour. Exponential models the continuous gap between those same events. Student's t looks like a normal curve but with heavier tails, reflecting the extra uncertainty of estimating spread from a small sample. Chi-square is built from sums of squared normal quantities and is right-skewed and non-negative, used to compare test statistics rather than to model raw data directly.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the normal distribution, per Lesson 12.
options: About 95 percent of values in a normal distribution fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
A z-score re-expresses a value as how many standard deviations it sits from the mean, which lets you compare values measured in different units.
scipy's stats.norm uses the parameter name scale to mean the variance, not the standard deviation.
A value more than 3 standard deviations from the mean is genuinely rare in a normal distribution, which is why such points are treated as candidate outliers.
Because a method like the t-test relies on the normal distribution, you should always assume your real data is normal without checking.
questions.explain: The 68-95-99.7 rule puts about 95 percent of values within 2 standard deviations of the mean. A z-score strips away units by expressing a value as a count of standard deviations from the mean, letting you compare unlike measurements on the same scale. Values beyond 3 standard deviations are rare under a normal curve, which is why they are flagged as outlier candidates. scipy's loc and scale parameters are the mean and the standard deviation respectively, not the variance. And the lesson explicitly warns that real data is never perfectly normal — check it with a histogram or Q-Q plot rather than assuming it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a distinctive feature of the Poisson distribution is that its mean and its ________ are both equal to lambda, the rate parameter.
questions.explain: The Poisson distribution has exactly one parameter, lambda, and both its mean and its variance equal lambda. If real count data shows a variance far larger than its mean (called overdispersion), Poisson is the wrong model for it.

questions.prompt: A data scientist draws 5,000 samples of size n=100 from a heavily right-skewed population of order values and plots a histogram of the 5,000 sample means. Based on the central limit theorem, what should that histogram look like, and why?
options: Roughly bell-shaped and centered near the population mean, even though the original order values themselves are right-skewed, because the CLT applies to the distribution of the sample mean, not to individual values.
Just as right-skewed as the original population, since averaging cannot change the shape of skewed data.
Centered near the population median rather than its mean, since skewed data pulls averages toward the middle value.
Roughly bell-shaped, but only if the original population happened to already be normal.
questions.explain: The CLT says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape as n grows, regardless of the original population's shape. Lesson 16 demonstrated exactly this with a right-skewed exponential population, where skewness of the sample means fell from about 1.8 at n=1 toward 0.24 at n=100 as the histograms became visibly bell-shaped. The CLT describes the behavior of averages, not a transformation of individual values, which remain just as skewed as ever.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because the standard error of the mean equals s divided by the square root of n, quadrupling the sample size shrinks the standard error to ________ of its original value.
questions.explain: Standard error scales with 1 over the square root of n. Quadrupling n means dividing by the square root of 4, which is 2, so the standard error roughly halves, exactly the pattern Lesson 17 highlights: quadrupling the sample roughly halves the standard error. This is also why gaining precision gets expensive: shrinking the SE by a large amount requires a disproportionately large increase in sample size.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about what a 95 percent confidence interval actually means, per Lesson 18.
options: The 95 percent describes the long-run success rate of the procedure: if you repeated the sampling and interval-building process many times, about 95 percent of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter.
For any one interval you have already computed, there is a 95 percent probability that the true population mean falls inside it.
A higher confidence level, such as 99 percent instead of 95 percent, produces a wider interval, all else equal.
A confidence interval corrects for a biased, non-random sample, so a biased sample and a random sample of the same size give equally trustworthy intervals.
Increasing the sample size, holding confidence level fixed, tends to narrow the interval.
questions.explain: The confidence level describes the long-run behavior of the method, not the probability for one specific interval. The true mean is a fixed number that either falls inside your one interval or doesn't, which Lesson 18's 2,000-trial simulation illustrated directly (about 94.75 percent of repeated intervals captured the true mean). A higher confidence level demands a wider interval, and a larger sample narrows it, both demonstrated with concrete widths in the lesson. A confidence interval only accounts for random sampling error; it cannot fix a biased sample, which can be confidently wrong regardless of its width.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the bootstrap procedure, per Lesson 19, in the correct order.
items: Start with your one original sample of n observations
Draw n observations from that sample with replacement to create one bootstrap resample
Compute the statistic of interest (such as the mean or median) on that resample
Repeat the resampling and computing step thousands of times to build a distribution of the statistic
Read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that distribution off as a 95 percent confidence interval
questions.explain: The bootstrap starts from the one sample you actually have, since you cannot go back and collect more. Each resample draws n observations from that same sample with replacement, so some values repeat and others are left out. The statistic is recomputed on each resample, and repeating this thousands of times builds up an approximate sampling distribution. Finally, taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of all those resampled statistics gives the percentile-method 95 percent confidence interval, exactly as Lesson 19 computed for both a mean and a median.

questions.prompt: A company surveys 20,000 customers by email and finds average satisfaction is much higher than internal records suggest it should be. Only customers with 6 or more purchases a year tend to respond. According to Lesson 15, will collecting even more email responses from the same process fix this discrepancy?
options: No — this is selection bias, a systematic tilt from who chooses to respond, and more data from the same biased process only makes the wrong estimate more precise, not more accurate.
Yes — sampling variability shrinks as sample size grows, so with enough responses the estimate will converge on the truth.
Yes, but only if the company also doubles the number of questions in the survey.
No, because email surveys are always invalid regardless of who responds.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 draws a sharp line between random sampling error, which shrinks and averages out as a sample grows, and sampling bias, a systematic tilt caused by how the data was collected. The heavy-purchaser response pattern described here is exactly the selection-bias example from the lesson, where collecting 2,000 respondents from the same biased group did not repair the estimate — it only made the company more precisely wrong. Fixing bias requires a better collection design, not more volume.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Type I error from a Type II error in hypothesis testing?
options: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false alarm), with probability alpha; a Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a miss), with probability beta.
A Type I error is failing to reject a true null hypothesis; a Type II error is rejecting a false null hypothesis.
A Type I error and a Type II error both describe the same mistake, just under different names used by different fields.
A Type I error's probability is beta; a Type II error's probability is alpha.
A Type I error can only happen when the null hypothesis is actually false.
A Type II error is impossible once a result is declared statistically significant.
questions.explain: A Type I error means claiming an effect that isn't really there, rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true, and its probability is alpha, the significance level set in advance. A Type II error means missing a real effect, failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, and its probability is beta. Power, 1 minus beta, is the chance of correctly detecting a real effect.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes two outcomes that don't exist in this framework as errors at all: failing to reject a TRUE null and rejecting a FALSE null are both correct decisions, not mistakes. Only rejecting a true null (a false alarm) or failing to reject a false null (a miss) count as the two kinds of wrong decision, so option B swaps which outcomes are actually the errors.

questions.prompt: A junior analyst runs a two-sample t-test and reports: 'the p-value was 0.03, so there is a 97 percent chance our new checkout page is actually better.' What is wrong with this statement, per Lesson 21?
options: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability that the alternative hypothesis (or the null) is true, so the 97 percent figure is a misreading of what the test computed.
Nothing is wrong; a p-value of 0.03 is mathematically identical to a 97 percent chance the effect is real.
The statement is wrong only because the analyst should have used a one-sided test instead of a two-sided one.
The statement is wrong because a p-value of 0.03 actually means there's a 3 percent chance the new page is better.
questions.explain: The p-value answers 'how likely is data this extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true' — it says nothing directly about the probability that the null or the alternative hypothesis is true. Getting an actual probability for a hypothesis requires Bayes' theorem and a prior, which a p-value alone does not supply. Lesson 21 specifically calls out 'there is a 96.5 percent chance the effect is real' as one of the most common misreadings of a p-value of 0.035.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about choosing the right t-test, per Lesson 23.
options: A paired t-test should be used when the same customers are measured before and after a change, since it analyzes the per-customer differences rather than treating the two sets of measurements as unrelated groups.
Welch's two-sample t-test (equal_var=False) is a safer default than the classic Student's t-test when the two groups might have different variances.
Treating paired, before-and-after data as two independent groups instead of running a paired test can only ever increase statistical power, never reduce it.
A one-sample t-test compares a single group's mean against a fixed reference value.
scipy's ttest_ind always assumes equal variances between the two groups and provides no way to relax that assumption.
questions.explain: A paired test is for matched measurements, like the same customers before and after a program, and analyzing per-customer differences removes the customer-to-customer variation that can otherwise drown a real effect. Lesson 23 showed the paired test finding p=0.0011 while treating the same data as independent groups gave p=0.2509 and missed the effect entirely, the opposite of 'can only increase power.' Welch's test, by not assuming equal variances, is recommended as the safer default for two independent groups. A one-sample t-test checks a single group's mean against a fixed value, like a 3.0-day delivery promise. And ttest_ind explicitly supports equal_var=False to relax the equal-variance assumption via Welch's test.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: power is defined as 1 minus ________, the probability of a Type II error.
questions.explain: Beta is the probability of a Type II error, missing a real effect. Power is defined as 1 minus beta: the probability of correctly detecting a real effect of a given size, with 80 percent being a common target.

questions.prompt: Match each hypothesis-testing tool to the situation it is built for, per Chapter 5.
right: Comparing three or more group means at once using between-group versus within-group variability
Testing whether two categorical variables are related using a table of observed versus expected counts
Controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries across many tests, at the cost of less strictness than Bonferroni
Comparing the same subjects' measurements before and after a change by analyzing per-subject differences
questions.explain: A paired t-test analyzes matched before/after measurements on the same subjects. A chi-square test of independence compares observed counts in a two-way table against the counts expected if the two categorical variables were unrelated. One-way ANOVA compares three or more group means via the ratio of between-group to within-group variability (the F statistic). Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of false positives among flagged results, which is more lenient than Bonferroni's stricter family-wise error control.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the hypothesis-testing recipe, per Lesson 20, in the correct order.
items: State the null hypothesis (H0) and the alternative hypothesis (H1) before looking at the results
Choose a test statistic that measures the gap you care about
Determine how often chance alone would produce a statistic at least this extreme, assuming H0 is true
Reject H0 if that probability is small enough, or otherwise fail to reject it
questions.explain: The recipe always starts by stating both hypotheses before looking at results, so the question is locked in ahead of time. Next you pick a test statistic that captures the gap you're investigating. Then you work out how surprising a result this extreme would be if the null hypothesis were really true, the step a permutation test performs by brute-force shuffling and a formula-based test performs with math. Only then do you make the reject-or-not decision based on how small that probability is.

questions.prompt: A support team notices that in months when they hire more temporary agents, customer complaint volume is also higher, with a strong positive correlation. Someone proposes hiring fewer agents to reduce complaints. Based on Lesson 27, what is the most likely flaw in that reasoning?
options: Both hiring and complaint volume are probably driven by a third variable, such as holiday-season order volume, which is a confounder that creates the correlation without either variable causing the other.
The correlation proves that hiring more agents directly causes more complaints, so reducing headcount is the correct fix.
The correlation is meaningless because correlation coefficients can only be computed on categorical data.
The team should ignore the correlation entirely, since correlation is never relevant to planning staffing.
questions.explain: The pattern matches Lesson 27's ad-spend-and-sales example exactly: a seasonal driver (there, the holiday season; here, order volume) can push both variables up at once, producing a strong correlation with no causal link between them at all. Cutting agents because of this correlation would be a mistake, since the real driver is the volume of orders needing support, not staffing levels causing complaints. The fix is to look for the confounder, not to act on the raw correlation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about simple linear regression, per Lesson 28.
options: R-squared tells you what share of the outcome's variation is accounted for by the predictor, and in simple regression it equals the correlation coefficient squared.
A fitted regression line can be trusted to predict outcomes for x-values well outside the range of the original data, since the same line keeps holding.
The slope describes association between x and y, and does not by itself prove that changing x would cause a change in y.
The least squares method chooses the intercept and slope that minimize the sum of the squared residuals.
If a plot of the residuals shows a clear curve or funnel shape, that is evidence the straight-line model fits the data well.
questions.explain: R-squared is literally the correlation coefficient squared in simple regression, and it measures the share of outcome variation explained by the predictor. The slope only describes an association found in the data; it doesn't by itself establish that changing x would cause a change in y. Least squares is defined as the method that minimizes the sum of squared residuals. Extrapolating beyond the observed range of x is explicitly warned against, since the relationship may not hold there. And a curved or funnel-shaped residual plot is a sign the line is the wrong model, not evidence the fit is good.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in A/B test design, the smallest lift you would actually care about detecting is called the minimum detectable ________.
questions.explain: The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest lift worth caring about, for example moving conversion from 10 percent to 12 percent. It is a business decision as much as a statistical one, since smaller MDEs require dramatically larger sample sizes, as Lesson 29 showed with the jump from 3,841 users per group to detect a 2-point lift up to 14,751 to detect a 1-point lift.

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, treatment converts better than control within both the desktop segment and the mobile segment individually, yet control wins when the two segments are combined into one overall number. What does Lesson 31 say is the most likely explanation?
options: An uneven mix of segments across the two groups, for example treatment having a much larger share of a lower-converting segment than control, which is Simpson's paradox.
The test must contain a calculation error, since a treatment that wins every individual segment must also win overall.
This always means the sample size was too small to trust any of the numbers.
The result shows that chi-square tests cannot be used on segmented data.
questions.explain: This is exactly the Simpson's paradox example from Lesson 31: treatment won inside both the desktop and mobile segments individually, but lost overall because most treatment users happened to be drawn from the lower-converting mobile segment. The reversal comes from an uneven mix of segments across groups, not from a calculation error, which is also why checking segment balance after randomization matters.

questions.prompt: The capstone's pre-analysis plan tests two outcomes (90-day churn and 90-day spend) and applies a Bonferroni correction. The churn test returns p = 0.015 and the spend test returns p = 0.88. Using the corrected threshold, what is the correct conclusion?
options: The threshold becomes 0.05 / 2 = 0.025; churn's p-value of 0.015 passes this stricter bar while spend's p-value of 0.88 does not, so only the churn result can be called a win under the plan.
Both results pass, since 0.05 is the only threshold that ever matters regardless of how many outcomes are tested.
Neither result passes, since Bonferroni correction always rejects every test when more than one outcome is measured.
The threshold becomes 0.05 x 2 = 0.10, so both p-values comfortably pass.
questions.explain: Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests, so testing two pre-registered outcomes at an overall alpha of 0.05 means each individual test needs p below 0.05/2 = 0.025 to count as a win. The capstone's churn result (p = 0.015) clears that bar; the spend result (p = 0.88) does not, so the write-up reports a churn reduction that survives correction and a spend effect that remains undetectable, exactly the conclusion Lesson 33 reaches.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the stakeholder-summary template from Lesson 34 to what belongs in it.
right: State what to do next, such as rolling out the change while continuing to track the metric
Lead with the answer in plain language, such as the size of the churn reduction observed
Note the limits of the analysis, such as a wide confidence interval or a short measurement window
Describe the method and the numbers that back up the headline, such as the experiment's design and its confidence interval
questions.explain: The template leads with the headline answer in plain language, then backs it up with the evidence (the experiment's design and its confidence interval), then states caveats such as a wide interval or a measurement window that only covers 90 days, and finally closes with a concrete recommendation for what to do next. Lesson 34 stresses leading with the answer first rather than reciting a p-value, since the write-up is often the only thing a reviewer actually reads.
